notes:
I've written verse-by-verse notes for Jude 1 below. I ran out of searches before I could cover everything:

- **Fully covered:** vv. 1–5, plus the main debates on v. 4 (what "designated long ago" means), v. 5 ("Jesus" or "Lord"), vv. 9 and 14–15 (Jude's use of books outside the Bible) and vv. 21/24 (can a believer fall away).
- **Thin:** vv. 6–8, 10–13 and 16–25 are covered only from short search excerpts.
- **Not found:** v. 7 has no exposition beyond a one-line summary, and v. 13 has nothing.
- **Missing views:** I found no Pentecostal reading of "praying in the Holy Spirit" (v. 20), no Lutheran or Orthodox material, and no netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes.
- **Some names left out:** a few comments appear on pages that quote several older commentaries side by side. Where I couldn't tell who wrote a line, I left the name out.

**v. 1**
- Jude is the half-brother of Jesus named in Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3. He didn't believe in Jesus as the Messiah until after the resurrection, and he chose the humbler title "bondservant" over his family tie. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- Swindoll argues that "brother of James" means he probably wasn't the apostle Jude, who was the "son of James" in Luke 6:16. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary
- Spurgeon reads the greeting as the whole work of salvation in brief: set apart by the Father, joined to and kept in Christ, called by the Spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary
- Matthew Henry leaves open whether "brother" is meant "in the strictest or a larger (though very usual) acceptation." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jud/Jud_001.cfm
- Schaff's encyclopedia agrees the James meant is the Lord's brother. It adds that v. 17 suggests Jude was not one of the Twelve. https://ccel.org/s/schaff/encyc/encyc06/htm/iii.lvii.cxlv.htm
- Precept Austin, quoting Wuest, says "loved" is a perfect tense: believers stay permanently loved by the Father. The Father keeps them so they remain Christ's possession forever. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary

**v. 2**
- Paul usually greets with "grace and peace"; Jude's greeting is different in wording but much the same in substance. Jude wants these blessings multiplied, not just added. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/

**v. 3**
- Jude meant to write about salvation but felt pressed to write a warning instead. "Contend" is a wrestling word, a strengthened form of "agonize," and its tense shows an ongoing struggle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- "The faith" means the core gospel truths all Christians share, not personal belief. "Once for all" means it was delivered through the apostles and prophets and won't be added to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- MacArthur pictures a soldier guarding a holy treasure. He says the readers' own salvation was not at risk. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary
- Matthew Henry says to contend as the apostles did: by suffering patiently for the truth, "not by making others suffer". He adds that the essentials are plain enough that no "infallible interpreter" is needed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jud/Jud_001.cfm

**v. 4: the traditional reading**
- The danger is that these men went unnoticed. Twisting grace this way doesn't make grace dangerous; "It simply shows how corrupt the human heart is." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- Matthew Henry: turning grace into an excuse for sin amounts to denying both natural and revealed religion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jud/Jud_001.cfm

**v. 4: where traditions differ ("designated long ago for condemnation")**
- **Reformed:** Calvin sees God's eternal counsel behind the phrase, pictured as a book. He also says Jude wanted to reassure readers that the church is tested only by God's "infallible counsel." https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol45/htm/viii.iii.htm
- **Reformed:** Gill rejects reading it as a reference to earlier prophecy. He takes it as an eternal decree ("reprobation is of the same date with election") that does not make God the author of sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jude/1-4.htm
- **Reformed:** The Geneva notes say it is by God's providence, not chance, that wicked men creep in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jude/1-4.htm
- **Non-Calvinist:** Barnes says the word "of old" cannot prove the ordination was eternal, so the verse shouldn't be used for an arbitrary decree of destruction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jude/1-4.htm
- **Non-Calvinist:** Another commentary quoted on the same page adds that "of old" is never used of God's eternal counsels. It says the Greek verb suggests a public notice, giving the sense "marked out as on their way to this condemnation." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jude/1-4.htm
- **Non-Calvinist:** The Pulpit Commentary prefers "written of" in ancient prophecy over the Calvinist "foreordained." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jude/1-4.html
- StudyLight lists Wesley's Notes under its Arminian heading for this verse; I couldn't read Wesley's own comment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jude/1-4.html
- **Text note:** some Greek copies add "God" in this verse (as the NKJV does). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21435

**v. 5**
- **Textual question ("Jesus" or "Lord"):** Monergism judges "Jesus" most likely original. It cites the earliest manuscripts and the likelihood that scribes changed "Jesus" to "Lord." It notes the ESV, CSB, NET and NLT read "Jesus," while the KJV, NKJV and NASB95 read "Lord." https://www.monergism.com/reformation-theology/blog/jesus-who-saved-people-out-land-egypt-jude-5
- Ellicott calls "Jesus" a remarkable reading, showing the man Jesus identified with the eternal Son. https://biblehub.com/jude/1-5.htm
- Utley lists the many variant readings and puts them down to "Lord" being ambiguous between persons of the Trinity. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21435
- The Catholic Douay-Rheims reads "Jesus." https://biblehub.com/esv/jude/1-5.htm
- **Meaning:** Israel's judgment shows these men will be judged even if they started well. It also warns us that past experience doesn't guarantee future faithfulness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- Israel's root failure was unbelief, and persevering means continuing to believe to the end. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary
- Matthew Henry calls 1 Corinthians 10:1–10 the best commentary on this verse. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jud/Jud_001.cfm

**v. 6**
- Guzik links these angels to an "unnatural union" that led God to imprison them in a special way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- Their present confinement isn't their final place; that will be assigned on the great day. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary
- Calvin compares them to military deserters who left their post. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jude-1.html
- Berkhof notes some think this verse also draws on the Book of Enoch. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/berkhof/newtestament.xxxii.html

**v. 7**
- I found only a one-line summary. The Catholic Encyclopedia lists Sodom with Israel and the angels as proof the false teachers will be punished. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/epistle-of-saint-jude

**v. 8**
- Guzik ties these men to Sodom by their sensuality and their rejection of God's authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- **"Glorious beings":** Schreiner says some take these as good angels. He prefers evil angels, because in v. 9 Michael won't pass his own judgment on the devil. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary
- Wesley instead takes "authority" to mean those Christ has made overseers of his flock. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/jude-1.html

**v. 9**
- Matthew Henry: Michael wasn't afraid of the devil. He thought trading insults with him beneath him, a lesson never to use railing in disputes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jud/Jud_001.cfm
- **Source of the story:** The Catholic Encyclopedia notes early writers including Origen traced it to the *Assumption of Moses*, though Jude may have known it from Jewish tradition. It says Jude doesn't quote that book as a written authority, still less as Scripture. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08542b.htm
- Berkhof retells the *Assumption* version, in which Satan claimed the body because Moses had committed murder. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/berkhof/newtestament.xxxii.html
- Utley says the verse shows Michael respecting Satan's position, and that "Lord" here means YHWH. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21435

**v. 10**
- These men claimed to be spiritual, but their knowledge was only "natural," and they corrupted themselves even with that. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- Green: a man who keeps refusing God's call is eventually left to the instincts he once chose as freedom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary

**v. 11**
- Cain's way is unbelief and empty religion, leading to jealousy and murderous anger. His offering was rejected because it wasn't offered in faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- Wesley notes Jude is the only apostle to pronounce a "woe." He says "rushed headlong" literally means "poured out," like a flood with no banks. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/jude-1.html

**v. 12**
- Calvin: like clouds driven by wind, these men promise much but are empty inside. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jude-1.html

**vv. 14–15**
- Hiebert: Jude appeals to prophecy to show their judgment is already set. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary-2
- Wesley says sinners are bad, but the ungodly who sin without fear are worse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/jude-1.html
- **Use of Enoch:** Many Catholic scholars see a loose quotation of the Book of Enoch, but Jude does not quote it as canonical. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08542b.htm
- The ISBE compares Paul quoting Epimenides (Titus 1:12–13): quoting a non-biblical book doesn't endorse the whole book. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/isb/j/jude-the-epistle-of.html
- Jerome reports that some early Christians rejected Jude because of the Enoch quotation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/search/dictionary/viewtopic.cfm?topic=IT0005207
- McClintock and Strong say it isn't certain Jude used the book as we now have it. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/j/jude-epistle-of.html

**v. 16**
- Pentecost sums the false teachers up as loudly discontented, self-centred, boastful and flattering. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary-2
- Guzik notes their methods all revolved around words. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/

**vv. 17–18**
- Nothing about these men should have surprised the readers; the apostles had warned of them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary-2
- The scoffers may be those who mock Christ's return, or those who mock believers who won't follow them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says Jude speaks of the apostles as a group because they were scattered in different places, not because they lived long before. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/epistle-of-saint-jude

**v. 19**
- These men think themselves the truly spiritual ones, but in fact they lack the Spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary-2

**v. 20**
- Bauckham calls vv. 20–23 the climax of the letter. Lloyd-Jones calls praying in the Spirit "the secret of true prayer." https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_20_commentary
- Guzik: we grow *on* the foundation of the faith, and no one else can grow for you. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/

**v. 21: where traditions differ (can a believer fall away?)**
- **Baptist/Reformed-leaning:** Precept Austin sets God keeping us (vv. 1, 24) beside our duty to keep ourselves. It says "Jude clearly believes that no genuine believer will ever lose his or her salvation." https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_21_commentary
- **Calvary Chapel / Pentecostal-leaning:** Guzik stresses that past experience doesn't guarantee future faithfulness, so we must keep walking and stay on guard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
- **Methodist:** Barclay quotes Wesley: "Let, therefore, none presume on past mercies, as if they were out of danger." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jude/1-15.html
- Matthew Henry says eternal life comes only through mercy, not our own merit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jud/Jud_001.cfm

**v. 22**
- Moo warns we can't be completely sure what Jude wrote in vv. 22–23, because the manuscripts differ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_22_commentary
- Constable says these are sincere doubters to be restored gently, not abandoned. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_22_commentary

**v. 23**
- Sidlow Baxter says some deceived people need urgent rescue. With others we must be careful not to stain our own garments. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_commentary

**v. 24**
- God's keeping in v. 1 and here frame our duty to keep ourselves in v. 21. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_24_commentary
- In the end, it is God who keeps us from stumbling. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/

**v. 25**
- "God our Savior" here means the Father: the Father starts salvation, the Son accomplishes it, and the Spirit applies it. Kistemaker links the verse to *Soli Deo Gloria* ("to God alone be the glory"). https://www.preceptaustin.org/jude_25_commentary
- We don't add glory to God; we glorify him by declaring what is true of him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/

**Popular modern teaching (hyper-grace)**
- I found no page that addresses modern hyper-grace teaching by name. Two related points:
  - On v. 4, Guzik says the danger lies in people twisting grace, not in the message of grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jude-1/
  - Barclay describes the false teachers as self-styled spiritual people who thought sin didn't apply to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jude/1-15.html
